## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the Statement and [A1], [F1]–[F4].

1.1 On any input where the algorithm returns numerical estimates, each propensity ratio is finite: when $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)>0$, it is a quotient of finite probabilities by a positive probability; when both probabilities are zero, the algorithm sets the ratio to zero. If $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)=0<\pi(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)$, the algorithm returns `unsupported` instead. Thus every cumulative weight is finite. Each return and every finite sum in OIS and PDIS is finite because the reward set, horizon, and dataset are finite. The WIS numerator and denominator are finite, and the procedure either divides by a positive finite denominator or returns zero. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 An observed pair with $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)=0$ lies on a behavior-null trajectory atom by [F1]. Since the trajectory space, horizon, and sample size are finite, the event that any observed pair has zero behavior propensity is a finite union of null events. The algorithm therefore returns numerical estimates almost surely under the behavior sample law. Extending the three estimator expressions by any fixed finite values on the `unsupported` null event does not change their expectations. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Fix a logged trajectory index $i$. By [F1], its law is $P^\mu_H$, and [F3] applied to $G_i$ gives $\mathbb E_\mu[W_{i,H-1}G_i]=\mathbb E_\pi[G_H]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Linearity [F4] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat J_{\mathrm{OIS}}]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_H(\pi;s_0)=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 Fix $i$ and $0\le t<H$. The reward $R_{t+1}^i$ is a function of the prefix through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[W_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i]=\mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1}]$. Multiplying each equality by the fixed $\gamma^t$ and summing the finite range $0\le t<H$, [F4] yields $\mathbb E_\mu[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tW_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 Each of the $n$ PDIS trajectory scores in [F2] has expectation $J_H(\pi;s_0)$ by step 2.2. Their finite sample average has the same expectation by [F4], proving $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat J_{\mathrm{PDIS}}]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Step 2.1 proves the ordinary-estimator claim. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, F2, F4, algebra] ∎

source_proposals.source_excerpt: They do not certify finite variance, a confidence bound, or that the target policy outperforms the behavior policy.
source_proposals.proposed_replacement: In this finite trajectory setting their finite numerical outputs have finite variance, but they do not provide a variance bound uniform over behavior policies, a confidence bound, or a guarantee that the target policy outperforms the behavior policy. For each fixed model, horizon, and sample size, the trajectory dataset space is finite; after any fixed finite assignment on the behavior-null unsupported event, each estimator has finitely many finite values, so its second moment and variance are finite.
